choices.text: 10, the same as the population standard deviation

questions.explanation: The sampling distribution of the mean keeps the population mean 60, but its standard deviation shrinks by root n: 10 / root 25 = 10 / 5 = 2. Larger samples give steadier means.
questions.prompt: A population has mean 60 and standard deviation 10. Samples of size n = 25 are taken. What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean?

questions.answer: Do not reject the null hypothesis. The p-value 0.31 is greater than alpha = 0.05, so the data is not surprising enough under the null to reject it.
questions.explanation: The verdict is always p against alpha: reject the null only when the p-value is smaller than the significance level. Here 0.31 > 0.05, so there is insufficient evidence against the null - which is not the same as proving the null true.
questions.prompt: A hypothesis test at the 5% significance level returns a p-value of 0.31. State the test verdict and give the reason.

questions.answer: A Type I error rejects a true null: declaring the machine miscalibrated when it is actually fine. A Type II error accepts a false null: passing the machine when it is actually miscalibrated. Alpha caps the probability of a Type I error.
questions.explanation: Type I is the false alarm - reject a true null - and its probability is the significance level alpha, chosen in advance. Type II is the missed signal - accept a false null - with probability beta, reduced by increasing the power 1 - beta, for example with a larger sample.
questions.prompt: In a quality test, the null hypothesis says a machine is calibrated. Describe a Type I error and a Type II error in this context, and state which error's probability is capped by the significance level alpha.
